Host
HōST
n. (rendering Hebrew tsābā', Greek stratia)
From Old French host, from Latin hostis, originally a stranger and then an enemy, whence hostilis — the army being the stranger-band that comes against you. (The English word for one who entertains guests is a separate line, from Latin hospes.) The Hebrew tsābā' means an organised body mustered for service, whether soldiers, labourers, or the ordered ranks of the stars, and it is the word in the divine title LORD of hosts.

Biblical Definition

Host is Scripture's word for an ordered array under command, and its range is the measure of God's dominion. It is first used not of armies but of the finished creation: “Thus the heavens and the earth were finished, and all the host of them” (Gen 2:1) — sun, moon, and stars conceived as ranks drawn up, each in its station. From that the divine title follows, and it is the great name of God's sovereignty in the historical books and prophets: “Who is this King of glory? The LORD of hosts, he is the King of glory” (Psa 24:10). The hosts are angelic as well as stellar, and the shepherds saw them mustered: “And suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host praising God” (Luk 2:13). Joshua, surveying Jericho, learns that the LORD's host has its own Captain who takes no side but His own: “Nay; but as captain of the host of the LORD am I now come” (Jos 5:14), and Joshua falls on his face and worships — a thing no created angel accepts. The title becomes a weapon in the mouth of faith when David refuses Goliath's terms and states the real disparity of forces: “Thou comest to me with a sword, and with a spear, and with a shield: but I come to thee in the name of the LORD of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom thou hast defied” (1Sa 17:45). To confess the LORD of hosts is to say that every ordered power in heaven and earth is already mustered and already commanded.

Webster 1828 Definition

An army; a great number arrayed for war; the ordered ranks of the heavenly bodies and of the angels; and in the divine title LORD of hosts, the sovereign Commander of every marshalled power in heaven and earth.

expand to see more

HOST, n. 1. An army; a number of men embodied for war; a great company.

2. Any great number or multitude; as a host of enemies, a host of friends.

3. The heavenly bodies, conceived as an ordered array; the host of heaven, the sun, moon and stars. Deut. 4.

4. The angels, as the armies of God; the heavenly host. Luke 2.

5. In the title LORD of hosts, Jehovah Sabaoth, the God who commands all the armies of heaven and earth. Psalm 24; 1 Sam. 17.

Key Scripture

Genesis 2:1 — "Thus the heavens and the earth were finished, and all the host of them."

Psalm 24:10 — "Who is this King of glory? The LORD of hosts, he is the King of glory. Selah."

Luke 2:13 — "And suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host praising God, and saying,"

1 Samuel 17:45 — "Then said David to the Philistine, Thou comest to me with a sword, and with a spear, and with a shield: but I come to thee in the name of the LORD of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom thou hast defied."

Modern Corruption

The LORD of hosts is treated as an embarrassing relic of tribal warfare to be quietly dropped, and the host of heaven is either mythologised into pagan astral religion or flattened into impersonal natural forces.

expand to see more

The title LORD of hosts occurs some two hundred and fifty times, and it is among the first casualties when a theology grows uncomfortable with divine power. It is presented as the residue of a warrior deity from Israel's primitive stage, outgrown by the fatherhood revealed in Christ. But the New Testament does not outgrow it; James takes the title untranslated into Greek and turns it against oppressive employers — the cries of them which have reaped are entered into the ears of the Lord of sabaoth — and Paul quotes Isaiah's except the Lord of Sabaoth had left us a seed as the ground of the remnant's survival. The title is not a rival to God's fatherhood but its guarantee: a father who cannot command the field cannot protect his children, and the comfort of the name lies exactly in the fact that the forces are His and are already drawn up.

The second corruption concerns the host of heaven. Because Israel's neighbours worshipped the stars, it is argued that Scripture's language of a stellar host is borrowed astral religion imperfectly demythologised. The texts say the reverse with unusual bluntness. The host of heaven is made — finished on the fourth day, ranked with the works of God's fingers — and Deuteronomy explicitly warns Israel against lifting up her eyes and being driven to worship them, because the LORD has divided them unto all nations. Scripture knows exactly what the nations did with the stars and forbids it by name. The principle to recover is that the heavens are an army under orders, not a pantheon and not a machine: they are personal enough to be commanded and impersonal enough that worshipping them is idolatry.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew tsābā' is an army, a mustered body, or organised service, used of soldiers, of the stars, and of the Levites' ministry; the plural gives Jehovah ts'bā'ōth, LORD of hosts. Greek stratia is an army or band of soldiers.

expand to see more

Hebrew tsābā' (H6635) — army, host, mustered service; used of warriors, of the host of heaven, and of the Levites' appointed service in the tabernacle.

Hebrew Jehovah ts'bā'ōth — the LORD of hosts; the great title of divine sovereignty, taken untranslated into Greek as sabaoth (Jas 5:4; Rom 9:29).

Hebrew ts'bā' hashshāmayim — the host of heaven; the ordered stars (Gen 2:1) and, in the prophets, the angelic court about the throne (1Ki 22:19).

Greek stratia (G4756) — an army, a band of soldiers; the heavenly host of Luk 2:13.

Greek archistratēgos — a chief captain of the host; the Septuagint title of the figure who met Joshua before Jericho (Jos 5:14).

Usage

"Of the finished creation as an ordered array: the heavens and the earth were finished, and all the host of them (Gen 2:1)."

"Of the divine title: who is this King of glory? The LORD of hosts, he is the King of glory (Psa 24:10)."

"Of faith's reckoning of the odds: I come to thee in the name of the LORD of hosts (1Sa 17:45)."
